https://www.cp24.com/news/world/2026/07/.text: LONDON — Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested Saturday in Miami after U.K. prosecutors said they brought further rape and sex trafficking charges against them. Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges relate to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The charges announced Saturday, which bring the total number of alleged victims in the U.K. to seven, are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the brothers that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have denied wrongdoing. Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers: Who the Tate Brothers are Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual U.S.-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny. Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines. He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer. The brothers are avid supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump. What the Tates are charged with Andrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the U.K. and Romania, where they moved to in 2016. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2010 and 2017. They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking. The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it “has requested the extradition of the Tates from the U.S. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the U.K.” The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. In June, a U.K. High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers. In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania. Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him. Why the Tates were in the U.S. British police previously sought the Tates’ extradition to the U.K. once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded. But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet. Romania’s foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania. Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates. Sylvia Hui, The Associated Press

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’ Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPA View image in fullscreen ‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’ Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPA Opinion Climate crisis We need a wartime mindset to fight the threat of wildfires Seth Klein While many leaders compare the wildfire crisis to the second world war, governments fail to adopt the real lessons of pre-emptive wartime action Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.09 EDT Share A s France and Spain battle historic wildfires , comparisons to the second world war abound. “One of the continent’s biggest evacuation efforts since World War II,” reports the Associated Press . The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has called the wildfires his country’s “ most difficult situation since the second world war ”. The images crossing all our screens certainly feel war-like – emergency aircraft and black smoke fill the skies, frantic civilians seeking shelter, historic towns lying in ruins, charred forests and burned-out vehicles, exhausted and sweat-soaked emergency responders. Of course, brutal fires such as these are not restricted to France and Spain. They are hitting much of Europe. Australia has wrestled with escalating heat and devastating wildfires for years; during the fires of early 2020, the Australian government was forced to deploy the most military assets since the second world war. The US has lost entire towns to these climate-induced infernos. Brazil, Greece, Portugal, Chile, Russia, Turkey, Indonesia … all know the terror and loss of the fiery new world in which we reside. Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George Monbiot Read more And in my own country, nearly a thousand wildfires are currently burning across Canada . In Europe , many leaders, including Macron and the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, have made a point of linking these fires to the climate emergency; in Canada and the US, decidedly less so. Less common still are leaders and media who connect these events to their primary source – our continued combustion of oil, gas and coal (with the Guardian and a few others being notably exceptions). Yet these extreme events leave no doubt: the climate emergency is upon us. The impacts of burning fossil fuels that climate scientists have warned of for years are now here. The province of British Columbia, where I live, seems to go through this every summer now. A few years ago, I recall arriving at a holiday spot my family has visited for many summers, and coming upon a scene unlike any we had ever experienced. Residents in the area had been put on evacuation alert. All afternoon, a fleet of four water-bomber float planes scooped up water from the lake directly in front of our rental house, flying in low over the homes in formation, collecting water in their pontoons and then doubling back to the fire on the mountain ridge behind us to dump their loads. Right up until sundown, four helicopters likewise circled back to the lake in five-minute rotations, dropping enormous buckets on long cords to collect water, and then racing back to the mountain to release their cargo. This continued all week. The noise was deafening. Our peaceful family time suddenly felt more like a scene from Apocalypse Now, as we huddled together and shouted to communicate. As darkness fell, the hills behind us were dotted with flames, and the sky glowed ominously red. This is what people now nervously call “the new normal”, although it is, in truth, not normal and but a taste of things to come. These extreme weather events we are increasingly experiencing – and the warlike mood they create – represent attacks on our soil. They are a call to mobilize. Sadly, however, the emergency-level responses we have seen to date are purely defensive, rearguard actions. Our governments have not yet seen fit to adopt a wartime-scale response that pre-emptively tackles the climate crisis. Beneath the urgency of the present lies a confounding paradox: we mobilize to put fires out, but not yet to prevent them. Sure, every time events like this occur, opinions flow freely about how we need to better prepare for fires, to make our communities and forests more resilient, and to adapt to this new reality. All true. But far too absent from the public debate is a more foundational truth: until we actually mobilize to dramatically expedite the transition off fossil fuels, we will never get ahead of the curve. No amount of fire preparation and planning will save us from an escalation in the horrors we are now experiencing. If the crisis before us is indeed akin to a war – and it is; an existential peril to the people and places we love – then we must genuinely adopt a wartime-scale approach, a new mindset to mobilize all of society, galvanize our politics, fundamentally remake our economy and end our dependence on fossil fuels. The good news: the second world war experience shared by many countries can be embraced as an instructive story, a helpful – and indeed hopeful – reminder that we have done this before. We have mobilized in common cause across society to confront a civilizational threat. And in doing so, we have retooled our entire economy in the space of a few short years. We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca Solnit Read more How does one know when a government is in actual emergency mode? From my studies of past mobilizations, real emergency action has certain distinct markers. Governments in genuine emergency mode: Tell the truth about the severity of the crisis and communicate a sense of urgency about the measures necessary to combat it. Spend what it takes to win. Create new economic institutions (state enterprises and public programs) to get the job done. Shift from voluntary and incentive-based policies to mandatory measures. Commit to leave no one behind. None of our governments are yet confronting the climate emergency in this manner. That time, however, will come. All emergencies start were a period of denial, or with a “phoney war” phase of half-hearted engagement (sound familiar?). But then, some sort of alchemy occurs. A combination of events (that’s what these extreme weather emergencies are) and leadership comes together to shift the zeitgeist and move us into genuine emergency mode. We need a “wartime” mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency. Seth Klein is a Canadian climate writer and activist, author of the book A Good War: Mobilizing Canada for the Climate Emergency , and former team lead of the Climate Emergency Unit . https://vietnamnews.vn/life-style/179978.text: Great National Unity Festival to be held abroad for first time PRAGUE — The first-ever Great National Unity Festival among overseas Vietnamese communities will be held in Prague, the Czech Republic, later this year, according to Guidance No. 12/HD-MTTW-BTT, dated September 11, 2026, by the Standing Board of the Việt Nam Fatherland Front (VFF) Central Committee. The festival aims to promote the traditions of the VFF, affirm the value of the great national unity bloc, and strengthen ties between Vietnamese communities abroad and the homeland. It is also intended to foster patriotism and national pride, encourage the preservation of the Vietnamese language and cultural identity, and inspire overseas Vietnamese (OVs) to contribute to national development. Prague was chosen due to the large Vietnamese community in the Czech Republic, where many live, study, and work. The festival will be a chance for associations, intellectuals, entrepreneurs, students, and other members of the community to connect and strengthen ties, fostering a united and well-integrated Vietnamese community. The festival will ideally be held around November 18, the traditional VFF day, alongside Vietnamese Culture Day on November 24. The schedule can be adjusted to suit local conditions and significant events related to the Vietnamese community or Việt Nam’s ties with the host country. The programme will comprise a ceremony and community activities. The ceremony will review the VFF’s traditions, highlight the significance of the festival and provide an overview of the Vietnamese community in the host locality. Representatives of Vietnamese diplomatic missions, associations and outstanding community members may share their experiences in community building, cultural and language preservation, and contributions to the homeland. Outstanding organisations and individuals will also be honoured for their contributions to community development, preservation of national cultural identity, Vietnamese-language teaching and learning, support for Vietnamese people abroad, promotion of Việt Nam’s image and national development. Community activities will feature cultural and artistic performances, including traditional costumes, folk songs and musical instruments, as well as regional cultural showcases, folk games and activities for young Vietnamese generations abroad. The festival may also include networking activities connecting overseas intellectuals, experts, entrepreneurs, young people and students with domestic agencies, localities and businesses, along with employment opportunities, innovation initiatives and Vietnamese products. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Josh Frydenberg may be at home in boardrooms and business lunches, but would he be able to win back the voters furious at ‘politics as usual’ and career politicians? Photograph: James Ross/AAP View image in fullscreen Josh Frydenberg may be at home in boardrooms and business lunches, but would he be able to win back the voters furious at ‘politics as usual’ and career politicians? Photograph: James Ross/AAP Coalition Analysis The return of the prodigal son? Why speculation is rising over Josh Frydenberg’s future Josh Butler The spectre of a leadership alternative is hardly helpful for Angus Taylor. But would Frydenberg do a better job? Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Tue 13 Oct 2026 03.09 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.01 EDT Share A reasonable query for Liberals at this point is: if Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question? There was a whiff of weariness in some corners of parliament this week, as the former treasurer and deputy Liberal leader happily stoked another round of “Josh for Canberra” speculation. With more rumoured comebacks than Oasis , Frydenberg’s latest foray into the national political arena saw him bouncing around TV, radio and podcast interviews to promote his new book, and pointedly refuse to rule out trying to rejoin the parliament. His book – part family history, part treatise on antisemitism and social cohesion, part political manifesto – is titled A Grateful Son. But is he instead the prodigal son? The one who set out on his own but is destined to be welcomed back to the Liberal party family with joy and celebrations? A Trump impersonator and opera singers: CPAC was a spectacle, but the right still can’t agree how to take down Labor Read more Frydenberg is young enough, bright enough and certainly energetic enough to still make a difference in public life. His addition to what is often a tired Coalition party room would certainly spice things up, and give a new weapon in its arsenal. The ideas in his book – a remix of the GST to fund income tax cuts, concerns about the future of his party, changes to the system of federalism, yet more calls for civic service for school leavers – are politically inconvenient for the federal Coalition as well as the Victorian Liberals headed for an election win, but are worth considering. The talk around parliament is that Frydenberg is privately telling people he is unlikely to seek a return. But the fact he has pointedly refused to rule it out in a conga line of media interviews, saying only that he would make his mind up later, seems opportunistic. The spectre of a potential leadership alternative is hardly a help for Angus Taylor . Labor sources have helpfully shared key quotes from Frydenberg’s book and media tour, pointing out his calls for changes to GST and the labour market, and criticisms of the Liberal trajectory – again, none helpful to the leader. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The problems facing the modern Liberal party, under Taylor’s leadership, are myriad. Its hostile right flank is barracking for Pauline Hanson and One Nation , its centre is still eyeing the teal independents, and Taylor – now eight months into the job – has a lower primary vote than Sussan Ley when she was dumped. The Guardian Essential poll found the Coalition primary vote at a record low 22% in September , compared to 25% in January , a fortnight before Taylor rolled Ley. These are all reasons for alarm for the centre right. It’s just not clear if Frydenberg is the answer to any of these problems. One question echoing around parliament this week was: would he do a better job than Taylor on anything substantive? In other words, is he yesterday’s man? A return to the party room would give the Coalition a well-known face and a policy brain in a team which could benefit from both. Maybe Frydenberg would be content to return as a loyal soldier under Taylor, serving in an appropriately senior cabinet role. But maybe not. Few think he’d give up a well-paid job in banking to sit on the frontbench instead of the leader’s chair. View image in fullscreen Josh Frydenberg outside the Treasury department building in Canberra in 2022. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP The loudest cheer Hanson got at last weekend’s Cpac conference was when she sledged Taylor, saying Australians didn’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. Would any of those voters more prefer the chair of investment bank Goldman Sachs, the role Frydenberg currently holds? Taylor in recent times has tried throwing a bone to that fringe of the rightwing movement, producing more off-the-cuff videos with unpolished deliveries (and swearing) a la Hanson – would Frydenberg, at home in boardrooms and business lunches, be able to win back the voters furious at “politics as usual” and career politicians? Maybe, then, Frydenberg could chart a course back to the middle for the Coalition: not chasing its right flank further to the fringe, but setting a mainstream course back toward the centre, where elections in Australia are won. That would be a decent idea, if you forget how Frydenberg was ejected from parliament in the first place: bundled out in 2022 by Monique Ryan in the big community independents wave which swept half a dozen moderate-ish urban Liberals from their seats. Ryan was supported by Climate 200 . That group’s origin story may be relevant here: Simon Holmes à Court, a former donor to Frydenberg’s Kooyong 200 fundraising vehicle, was reportedly ejected from a supporter event and set up his own group in response. Climate 200 would hardly respond to Frydenberg’s comeback, or potential leadership, with party poppers and a “welcome back” card. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion The teal wave that swept Frydenberg and several other moderate Liberals from office in 2022 hasn’t exactly swelled into a tsunami since then, and some could argue the conditions of four years ago are not there today – just ask Tim Wilson, who lost Goldstein to teal Zoe Daniel in 2022 but wrested it back in 2025. No Liberals we spoke to this week were jazzed about the prospect of Frydenberg’s return, or the distraction it provides. But if there were any people happy about his potential return, they were on the government benches. Albanese joked to Labor’s caucus meeting on Tuesday that Frydenberg was now the “shadow opposition leader”, claiming “Josh Frydenberg’s priority has always been Josh Frydenberg”. “I’m surprised Josh Frydenberg isn’t trying to bump me off this program,” the PM joked on the ABC later in the day. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, claimed his old sparring partner was “stalking” Taylor for the leadership. One senior Labor source cheekily joked that we should call it “the Fryre festival”, a reference to the ill-fated and chaotic Fyre festival in 2017 , which had its own short-lived and catastrophic comeback in 2024. Frydenberg’s media tour is likely to continue over coming days. The speculation over his potential comeback will linger even longer – Labor will make sure of it. https://www.politico.eu/article/investig.text: LONDON — Police are conducting a criminal investigation into a dispute connected to the founding of Your Party, a left-wing political party that was established last year. A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said it had launched an investigation after it received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database.” Officers recently arrested a man in his 20s on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, the spokesperson said. He was released pending further enquiries and has not been charged. Advertisement Advertisement Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” Scotland Yard did not name any political party in its statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party its investigation related to. However, three other people with knowledge of the circumstances, all of whom were granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing case, said the investigation relates to a long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. The left-wing party was co-founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons. The two MPs clashed publicly over a September 2025 email that was sent to around 800,000 people on the new party’s mailing list, encouraging them to sign up as paying members. Sultana had promoted the membership portal while Corbyn described its launch as “unauthorised.” Sultana later said her sole aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party.” Neither the man arrested, nor the woman interviewed by police, are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana are accused of wrongdoing. Advertisement Advertisement A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.” They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.” Isabel Loubser contributed reporting.
